members.statement: Define an intentional product personality and express it consistently through typography, color, corner shape, and interface copy.
When personality direction is unclear, study products familiar to the target audience for cues without copying direct competitors closely.
Create visual hierarchy by emphasizing the most important content and quieting lower-priority content instead of letting every element compete.
Use font weight and color as primary hierarchy tools, keep hierarchy palettes small, and avoid very light weights for small UI text.

Give every screen a clear visual hierarchy so the most important content stands out most and the least important least, letting a viewer deduce the structure from the layout and get instant clues about importance, relationships, and what to do next.

Establish a clear visual hierarchy by ranking controls and data from scenarios into instantly-needed, secondary, and by-exception, then distinguishing levels with hue, saturation, value, size, and position so the most important elements are larger and higher-contrast; adjust with restraint (often one property suffices, and prefer turning the less-important element down over turning the important one up), knowing a good hierarchy goes unnoticed while its absence causes glaring confusion.
On colored, patterned, or image backgrounds, reduce contrast with chosen related colors rather than generic grey text or translucent white text.
Solve accessible color contrast without overpowering hierarchy by flipping contrast or rotating hue before defaulting to very dark backgrounds or nearly white secondary text.
For text over photos, improve background consistency with overlays, contrast/brightness adjustment, colorization, or subtle text glow instead of only changing text color.
Decorate selected backgrounds with color, close-hue gradients, subtle patterns, or simple illustrations while keeping contrast low enough for content readability.

Make color choices legible first (dark on light or vice versa, verified by desaturating), and never rely on color alone: reinforce critical distinctions with shape and text because a significant fraction of users are colorblind.

Style actions by their page-level importance: make the true primary action prominent, keep secondary actions clear but quiet, and reserve destructive prominence for confirmation contexts where destruction is primary.
Avoid secondary actions where possible; when they must stay, reduce their prominence and visually distinguish them, and in wizards make forward a primary Continue and Back a secondary action.
Give each element or section only the width it needs, using narrow/mobile canvases and columns to avoid stretching content just because space exists.
Use grids as aids rather than mandates: prefer fixed or max-width sizing for content with an optimal width and percentage sizing only for elements meant to scale.
Adapt responsive sizes independently instead of preserving proportional ratios; large elements and component padding often need different scaling than small elements.
Respect the intended display size of icons, screenshots, logos, and favicons; use size-appropriate redraws, crops, simplifications, or containers instead of scaling detail beyond usefulness.
Leave letter-spacing at the typeface default unless tightening wide-font headlines or loosening all-caps text improves the specific use.

Choose typefaces by role (serif for dense body text, sans serif for UI and small sizes, display only for headlines, monospace for numeric/simple displays), keep on-screen type at least 10pt with 12pt standard body, set adequate leading, pair a serif with a sans serif, and left-align long text.
Keep body text readable: prefer sans serif at small sizes, avoid italic/ornamental/all-caps for long text, and set it in a medium column of about 10-12 words, ragged right.
Define fixed color shade scales from practical use cases, choosing base and edge shades first, filling the gaps, then refining by eye in real UI contexts.
Preserve color richness across shade scales by increasing saturation at lightness extremes, using modest hue rotation for perceived brightness, and deliberately warming or cooling greys.
Never make color the only carrier of meaning; pair it with another cue and use lightness contrast for color-vision resilience.
Use color intentionally for mood and emphasis (warm vs cool, high vs low contrast, saturated sparingly over a muted base) while avoiding eye-fatiguing combinations.

Convey meaning through the similarity and contrast of visual properties — users assume objects sharing properties are related and attend to the item of greatest contrast — choosing the property deliberately: size reads automatically as a hierarchy of importance and draws attention, shape best signals what an object is but is costly to attend to, hue must be used with a limited palette (never as the sole vector, given color-blindness), and texture is weak for differentiation but a strong affordance cue.
Create raised or inset depth by first deciding the intended surface profile, then applying subtle top-light highlights and shadows that preserve color quality.
In flat visual systems, communicate depth with relative lightness, darker inset surfaces, lighter raised surfaces, or short solid offset shadows.
Use shadows as a limited elevation system tied to focus and interaction, not as arbitrary decoration.
Use separate cast and contact shadows when one shadow cannot provide both broad elevation softness and edge definition.
Use colored accent borders as low-effort visual emphasis for cards, active navigation, alerts, headings, or layout edges.
Reach for fewer borders by using shadows, subtle background shifts, or extra spacing to separate elements when those cues are sufficient.

Treat each use of an application as a conversation the UI mediates, and design the software as a considerate conversation partner: understandable, signaling when it is active, obvious when responding, and offering anticipated next steps.

Apply the fifteen strategies for harmonious interaction as a checklist: follow users' mental models; less is more; enable users to direct rather than discuss; keep tools close at hand; provide modeless feedback; design for the probable and provide for the possible; provide comparisons; provide direct manipulation and graphical input; reflect object and application status; avoid unnecessary reporting; avoid blank slates; differentiate command from configuration; provide choices; hide the ejector-seat levers; and optimize for responsiveness while accommodating latency.

Provide direct manipulation and graphical input, not just graphical output, and reflect object and application status so a busy application looks busy and a sleeping one looks asleep, communicated through rich modeless feedback.

Design software to behave like a considerate, supportive human colleague, because people unconsciously treat interactive products as sentient and inconsiderate products irritate regardless of features, and it is not substantially harder to build, following the ideal division of labor in which the computer does the work and the person does the thinking.

Decide honestly whether most users will be perpetual beginners, occasional users, or experts, and design accordingly: optimize occasional/one-time interfaces for learnability (simplified, wizards, explained along the way) and frequent/expert interfaces for efficient operation.

Optimize the interface for perpetual intermediates, the large majority of users, devoting the bulk of effort to them while still letting beginners and experts be effective, with the threefold goal of moving beginners quickly into intermediacy, not obstructing intermediates who want to become experts, and keeping perpetual intermediates happy.

Support beginners without penalizing others: make beginner help removable rather than fixed in the interface, give beginners overview information such as scope and a guided tour rather than reference, reflect the user's mental model so concepts are grasped quickly, and treat users as intelligent but very busy by giving brief, targeted instruction plus cause-and-effect understanding.

Apply commensurate effort, since users work harder for what is more valuable to them, so an interface must not be complex to achieve simple results but may be complex to achieve complex, infrequent ones; organize controls and displays by frequency of use, degree of dislocation, and degree of risk exposure, and provide shortcuts for experienced users who will seek them.

Treat empirical research as the only reliable way to understand users: qualitative methods (interviews, direct observation, case studies) for expectations, vocabulary, and mental models, and quantitative methods (surveys) for numerical validation; even informal contact beats none.

Rely on qualitative research for how and why users behave, because quantitative market research and segmentation help sell products but fall short of revealing how people actually use them, and most traditional methods fail to translate research results into design solutions.
Use personas to model each user group's tasks, goals, and experience levels, and define target audiences by their task goals and behaviors rather than by marketing demographics.

Model users as personas, composite archetypes synthesized from observed behavior, and choose the primary design target by comparing goals and prioritizing the persona whose goals most broadly encompass those of the others.
Drive requirements from persona-goal scenarios rather than abstract tasks, and produce a requirements definition that balances user, business, and technical requirements.

Identify and prioritize user goals before tasks, and base the persona hypothesis on likely behavior patterns and their differentiating factors rather than purely on demographics, which should serve only as a proxy for behavior.

Organize the persona hypothesis by roles for business products but by attitudes, aptitudes, and behaviors for consumer products, and distinguish technical expertise from domain expertise, providing in-interface domain support when domain-naive users are in the target market.

After each interview compare and revisit notes and mark trends to feed persona creation, relying on the qualitative approach because it uniquely answers product questions at both the big-picture and functional-detail level with relatively little effort.

Use personas, research-based composite user models represented as specific individuals, to determine what the product should do, provide a common user-centered language, build consensus, reality-check the design at the whiteboard, and inform related marketing efforts.

Base personas on real-world observation, primarily in-context interviews, so almost every aspect traces to a user statement or behavior, and keep them context-specific, since personas generally cannot be reused across products even in a closely linked suite.

Distinguish persona archetypes from stereotypes, which reflect designer bias, by grounding demographics in data, making them typical and believable, erring toward diversity when data is inconclusive, and expressing exemplary behaviors within identified ranges.

Capture each persona's motivations as goals so that tasks can be improved or eliminated while still meeting the goal, and infer goals from qualitative data rather than asking users directly, expressing each goal as a single simple sentence, since a persona without goals is not a design tool.

Prefer personas over user roles, profiles, and market segments, and augment them appropriately: create customer and served personas for non-users, treat a user profile as a persona only if it is research-based, use market segments merely to filter interview scope, and fall back to clearly labeled provisional personas, drawn as sketches and documented, only when rigorous research is impossible.

Model three user-goal types, experience, end, and life goals, mapping to Norman's visceral, behavioral, and reflective levels: meet end goals for the product to be worth users' time and money, never egregiously violate experience goals since that alone dooms the product, and address life goals to turn a satisfied user into a loyal one.

Construct personas through the seven-step process, identifying behavioral variables (chiefly activities, attitudes, aptitudes, motivations, and skills), mapping each interview subject against them, finding significant behavior patterns as clusters of subjects across roughly six to eight variables with a logical connection, and synthesizing characteristics and goals from observed behavior.

Synthesize personas from observed behavior rather than fiction, keeping detail no deeper than the research supports, inferring goals from behavioral connections (about three to five end goals, zero or one life goal, zero to two experience goals), making each persona distinct in at least one significant behavior, expanding into a one-to-two-page narrative, and remembering personas are design tools, not an end in themselves.

Use narrative and persona-based scenarios as a primary creative design tool, with the persona serving as the tangible agent that keeps scenarios focused on goals rather than only tasks, and keep early solutions at the level of sketchy plot points.

Support Instant Gratification: make a new user's likely first action stunningly easy and deliver a success experience within the first few seconds, without blocking the first task behind registration, long instructions, slow loads, or ads, and deliver value before asking for something valuable in return.

Present only a few main entry points, task-oriented or audience-directed with clear calls to action, phrased in language first-timers understand, when a product has many first-time or infrequent users; skip this when the purpose is obvious to everyone and an extra step would irritate experts.

Support Streamlined Repetition: reduce repetitive operations to as few keystrokes or clicks as possible (find-and-replace, macros, scripting, copy-paste, shortcuts), using direct observation to discover repetitive tasks users will not report.

Offer Command History and Macros in complex tools so users can review, replay, and automate sequences (supporting streamlined repetition and flow), recording at the right granularity and constraining scriptable macros against abuse.

Treat information architecture as the invisible foundation and begin design there, especially for a new product: it is organizing and labeling the information space (structures, navigation paths, workflows, labels, search/browse/filter) so the product is understood and used with minimum mental strain.

Separate information from presentation by designing in layers (an IA foundation of concepts/labels/relationships, then a functionality layer, then a visual presentation layer), planning the information space from the user's point of view before locking into visual decisions.

Base information architecture on the users' vocabulary and mental model of the domain and design it to be evergreen: able to accept new content over time while still organizing everything without confusion.

For task and workflow apps, make frequently used tasks and controls immediately available without searching, hide rarely needed items behind navigation, and chunk large tasks into a sequence of steps that always shows the user where they are.

Minimize page-to-page jumps by keeping the structure as flat as possible with broad top-level (global) navigation, elevating frequently used actions for direct access, and structuring the app so the most common 80% of tasks complete on one screen without context switches.
Design a system of differentiated screen types (Neil's Overview, Focus, Make, Do) so users learn each screen reliably even as its content changes, and give each screen one clear organizing principle.

Maintain a consistent Visual Framework across all screens (shared layout, color, fonts, signposts) defined in a single place so style changes independently of content, because constants fade so changing content is noticed, and consistency lets users find things without relearning.

Support wayfinding with signposts and good signage: page/window titles, breadcrumbs, and progress indicators as 'you are here' cues; clear unambiguous labels where users expect them so no decision point lacks guidance; and place elements per environmental convention while remembering conventions are cultural.

Support navigation with reliable, consistent signposts such as menus and persistent objects, provide overviews like a thumbnail navigator or breadcrumb, use natural control-to-function mapping with terms that match users' mental models, and inflect the interface so the most frequently used functions are immediate while less used ones are pushed deeper without being removed.

Give controls clear affordance so an element looks or behaves like what it does, keep the visual language consistent (same icon or word means the same thing), and keep elements and text alignment stable from screen to screen.
Give elements room to breathe with margins and whitespace (crowding creates tension), use angles and curves to control calm versus motion, and keep textures subtle and away from small text.

Use photography to set mood and brand and icons to express function at a glance, following common icon conventions, keeping one icon style, avoiding decorative clutter in functional GUIs, and never relying on icons alone (pair with text labels).

Use cohesive, consistent, and contextually appropriate imagery grounded in the personas' mental models and cultural/domain visual language: give similar elements shared visual attributes and contrast only what differentiates meaning, design function-oriented icons that show both the action and the object acted upon, visually distinguish elements that behave differently with a consistent symbol per object type, and keep icons simple and schematic rather than photorealistic.

Build visual unity through repeated motifs (consistent angles, one body font, one headline font) applied only to comparable things, and choose a visual style (skeuomorphic, illustrated, flat, minimal) that fits the brand and the task.

Pursue visual simplicity and eliminate noise: avoid over-dimensional elements, heavy separators, insufficient whitespace, and overuse of color, texture, and contrast; use simple geometric forms, a restricted mostly-neutral palette with a few high-contrast accents, and one or two typefaces at a few sizes; treat unnecessary variation as the enemy by making near-equal sizes exactly equal and justifying every visual difference; and test each element's contribution by removing things until the design breaks, then restoring the last one.

Build accessibility in: support high-contrast themes and large fonts (often legally required), tone down loud visuals for long-use apps, and strip anything superfluous in high-stress interfaces where cognition outweighs aesthetics.

Design accessible forms by getting semantic content and structure right first (so assistive tech can convey them) and following core rules: text alternatives and labels for everything, unique meaningful links, never color alone, sufficient contrast, full keyboard operability, no seizure-risk flashing, adjustable timing, skip links, and naming objects by function—benefits reach all users.

Design mobile-first or responsive rather than shrinking the desktop site, because most users interact primarily on mobile, and know users' needs, tasks, and contexts before choosing between mobile web and a native app.

On tiny mobile screens strip the design to its essence and put the most relevant content high on the first screen (no layer-cake of logos, ads, and headers), keeping the most important functions on the front screen and burying or discarding the rest.

Make mobile touch targets large enough to hit (about 48x48 dp Android or 44x44 pt iOS with spacing, and make surrounding whitespace tappable), and minimize typing with autocompletion, prefills, and numeric entry.
Linearize mobile content into a single vertical column (labels above controls, degrade well at minimum width) and optimize the common sequences: minimize typing, screen loads, scrolling, and taps.

Design for the distracted, mobile context: support quick, reentrant, self-explanatory tasks; behave well in varied light, noise, motion, and social situations; and leverage device location and hardware.

For handhelds, integrate functionality to minimize navigation guided by context scenarios, validate the form with weighted physical models, design most data devices as satellites of a desktop, avoid floating and pop-up windows in favor of a full-screen sovereign style, and treat phones as transient with an arguably nonvisual best interface.

Before designing a list, analyze its use cases (overview, browse, search, sort/filter, rearrange) and nonvisual characteristics (length, order, grouping, item type, interaction, dynamic behavior), and choose order vs grouping by how users search.

Manage very long lists with Pagination (make the first screen enough, since most users will not go past it), an Infinite List for bottomless lists, an Alpha/Numeric Scroller for ordered lists, and a Find field plus filtering.

Choose where selected-item details appear by space and use case: Two-Panel Selector (details beside the list, best for overview/browse) for large screens, One-Window Drilldown (details replace the list) for constrained/mobile space, and List Inlay (details expand in place) when users compare items.

Prefer a Two-Panel Selector on large screens because it reduces physical effort, visual cognitive load (only the small area changes), and memory burden (the persistent list is a 'you are here' signpost), placing the list top/left and details below/right with keyboard navigation.

Make keyboard shortcuts, tab-order navigation, and direct manipulation available so users can operate without a mouse and act on objects directly (tap, swipe, drag, pinch), and make drag-and-drop work exactly as users expect or the illusion of direct manipulation breaks.

Provide an escape hatch during clicking and dragging — canceling a button press by moving off the control before release, or resetting a scrollbar when the drag strays too far — so users can recover from a mistake or change of mind, and reserve expert-only mouse idioms such as chord-clicking and double-click-and-drag for large sovereign applications with many selection permutations while sticking to basic actions for most products.

Understand drag-and-drop as clicking an object and moving it to imply a transformation, and provide strong visual feedback once a drag begins because, although users easily remember that an object can be dragged, they may forget the details of the action, while forgiving interactions and Undo encourage them to try direct manipulation without trepidation.

Choose the right action affordance for the job: buttons and button groups for always-visible related actions, links for low-emphasis actions, hover tools for per-item mouse actions, and an Action Panel for discoverable, richly organized commands; keep pop-up menus short and never use drop-downs for actions.

Use an iconic toolbar only when actions have obvious visual renderings, and always provide visible actions (buttons, links, menus) alongside any invisible ones (double-click, keyboard, CLI) so users can discover capabilities.

Design buttons to meet learned expectations: make a button visibly change from raised to indented when clicked (a painted button that does not move leaves users unsure their click registered), use links for navigation through content and buttons or butcons for actions and functions (users are confused when a link executes an action), and recognize that butcons suit intermediates because they are always visible and memorable but are unclear to novices, so provide ToolTips and prefer explicitly worded menus as the command vector for first-time users.

Let users instantly cancel a time-consuming operation with no side effects (cancel immediately and confirm it), because cancelability embodies user control and freedom and encourages safe exploration.

Make a process dialog satisfy four requirements — make clear a time-consuming process is happening, show through continual time-related movement that things are normal, indicate remaining time as progress relative to total, and provide a way to cancel and regain control — consider eliminating it by showing status in the main window (as a browser shows page-load progress) whenever the process is integral to that window, and make a Cancel button truly cancel by undoing everything so no trace remains, labeling it Stop instead if it only halts the operation partway.

Provide Multilevel Undo in highly interactive apps by modeling actions as reversible operations on a 10-12+ item stack, making reversible anything that could be permanent while leaving transient/view states untracked, defining operations in the user's terms, and exposing them with Smart Menu Items.

Discriminate incremental actions, which carry a data component (typing, cutting, pasting, deleting), from procedural actions, which have only a procedure (reformatting, rotating), because most Undo functions wrongly conflate them, and prefer explanatory Undo that labels the specific operation to be reversed (Undo Typing) over blind Undo, conveying the label through a ToolTip on a toolbar control.

Recognize the limits of stack-based Undo: single Undo is effective because it is simple, clear, and memorable (and its absence can drive users to abandon a product) but fails when a later trivial action short-circuits recovery of an earlier important one, while a strict last-in-first-out multiple-Undo stack models code and data structures rather than user goals and cannot reverse a discontinuous subset of interlaced actions while keeping the rest.

Design information graphics to show rather than tell and add interactivity so users explore and participate in discovery, first understanding what the user needs to learn (find a specific value vs understand structure).

Follow information-design principles for data displays: enforce visual comparisons, show causality and multiple variables, integrate text/graphics/data in one display, show states adjacent in space rather than stacked in time, and never de-quantify quantifiable data (show the actual numbers alongside trend graphics); above all ensure the quality, relevance, and integrity of shown content, and do not display information merely because it is technically possible, because poor-quality information damages user trust.
Support 'focus plus context' navigation of data (scroll/pan with an overview, zoom, drill-down, and search that pans to results) so users can focus on a point while keeping the big picture.

Make scrollbars informative — a thumb proportional to the visible portion, plus context such as total and current page as the user scrolls, and navigation tools like jump-to-start and bookmarks — and because scrollbars demand high mouse precision and poorly represent open-ended dimensions like time, consider a document navigator that gives a thumbnail overview and direct navigation when the document's big picture can be meaningfully represented visually.

Design forms to respect the user's time: make them short, minimize and deduce inputs, make the purpose clear (why, how used, what the user gets), minimize clutter, and confirm success with a clear next step.

Give a form strong vertical flow (aligned inputs, consistent spacing, top-aligned labels for responsive designs), group long forms into titled sections or show/hide sequences, and use descriptive labels and help while avoiding placeholder text that looks pre-filled.
Make the primary goal of every form to get people through it as quickly and painlessly as possible (Minimize the Pain), ideally so the form feels invisible.

Treat form design as high-leverage and measure its impact: expect substantial completion and revenue gains, and measure with multiple data sources (usability, field, support, tracking, eye-tracking, conventions), which need not be expensive.
Use a start page only for forms that demand substantial time or hard-to-gather information, stating what is needed and how long it takes; skip it when answers are readily available.

Prevent input errors and validate as early as possible: accept forgiving formats (echoing back the interpreted value) or structured-format fields for predictable data, offer input hints, prompts, autocompletion, and good defaults, and give actionable field-level validation before submission.

Place form error messages on the form itself, next to the offending field (never in a modal or on a separate post-submit screen), marked with color plus another cue, written short, specific, plain, and polite, validating client-side as focus leaves each field.

Prevent errors structurally: design the form to prevent them first (drop-downs for limited choices, few fields, clear required marking) and keep the submit control inactive until required steps are completed successfully.

Prefer data immunity over data integrity: do not validate and reject imperfect data at the point of entry (which puts the database's needs before the user's and treats the user as working for the application), but build applications smart enough to handle all permutations by looking before they leap, seeking help elsewhere in the system, and annotating problems; assume the user entered what he meant, and since incorrect input is often nearly correct, provide as much correction assistance and visual feedback on suspect entries as possible.

Keep data integrity from becoming the user's problem: accommodate the way humans think about partially or incorrectly filled-in documents, and where automatic correction silently changes input leave a visible mark or audit trail, making overly smart auto-formatting that can guess wrong easy to turn off and leaving the thinking to the human when it cannot be safely undone.

Solve input validation at the source by using bounded controls that communicate the acceptable boundaries and make an invalid entry impossible (a drop-down of months rather than requiring the user to spell February), rather than an unbounded field that accepts anything only to reject it afterward with a rude error; and where values are finite use a bounded numeric control such as a slider — good for relative or zoom values by analogy of position but poor for precise numbers, for which a spinner is better — or a list control, so users are not forced to type.

When an unbounded validation control is unavoidable, give generous rich modeless feedback rather than merely refusing input: visually distinguish validation controls from ordinary ones by typeface, border, or background; when active validation rejects a keystroke make clear that and why it did so; make passive validation responsive with a countdown timer, reset on each keystroke, that validates about half a second after the user pauses; explain the acceptable range in a clue box near the offending entry; and handle out-of-bounds data gracefully by converting a spelled value like nine into 9 or substituting the nearest allowable value while modelessly explaining the substitution.

Use good defaults and smart prefills to cut the user's work (from session, account, location, time, and safe inferences), but never prefill sensitive fields or pre-check advertising opt-ins, and require a conscious choice when the user must engage with the question.

Use smart defaults deliberately—defaults powerfully shape outcomes (e.g., organ-donor rates)—choosing preselected options that serve most people's interests to cut choices, aligning them with users (not the business) rather than opting people into unwanted options, deriving them from context, making them sticky for returning users, and omitting them when no option fits most people or the choice is sensitive.
Choose label alignment by goals and constraints: top-aligned for fastest completion and localization, right-aligned to save vertical space, left-aligned for scanning or to deliberately slow users.

Prefer top-aligned labels for speed: eye-tracking (Penzo ~50ms vs ~500ms left / ~240ms right) and live-site tests (>10% higher completion) show them fastest, and they flex for long/localized labels—accepting more vertical space, and noting the evidence is for familiar data.
Use right-aligned labels for fast completion when vertical space is tight, accepting that the ragged left edge and label wrapping reduce scannability.
Use left-aligned labels when scannability matters or data is unfamiliar, or deliberately to slow users down—accepting they are the slowest to complete.
Keep label alignment consistent within a single form, and weigh the context-versus-consistency trade-off across forms in one application.
Add help text only for specific triggers (unfamiliar data, why-asked, privacy concern, recommended format, unusual optional/required status) and keep it to the minimum needed.
Treat heavy help text as a red flag that questions are poorly phrased, too complex, or unnecessary, and never rely on instructions—eye-tracking shows people skip them and jump to the first input.

For help-heavy forms, use a dynamic help system: automatic inline help reveals content adjacent to a field on engagement (with a strong visual tie), while accepting its drawback that users cannot tell help exists until they start—best for answerable-but-uncertain questions.
Place help inside an input field only to hint at recommended answer formats (not to explain what/why/optional), ensuring it disappears on entry and is visually distinct from data.
Minimize optional fields, and when marking required/optional status indicate only the minority case with clear text (not just an asterisk), placing indicators next to labels for easy scanning.
On short forms you may thoughtfully omit either the top-level message or the per-input indicators, ensuring whatever remains has strong contrast.
Recognize that every form is built from three elements—labels (questions), input fields (answers), and actions (submission)—and design each in that role.

Build forms on rich semantic HTML (LABEL for a control, LEGEND/FIELDSET for a group), use CSS for layout, decompose complex structures into simple ones, avoid pixel-perfection across browsers, and separate a form's behavior from its presentation.

Match the input control to the question type (yes/no, single vs multiple mutually exclusive choices, free text), knowing each control's behavior and trade-offs: give radio buttons a default and clickable labels, use checkboxes for any-number choices, use drop-downs to save space but not for very long or familiar lists, avoid list boxes, and weigh click-efficiency vs error-prevention vs clarity.

Use selection controls correctly: let a selection control double as an imperative control only when users benefit from seeing the immediate, easily undone impact of their choice, otherwise require an explicit imperative control so users can make several selections before committing; keep check boxes square and radio buttons round per the learned standard shapes; avoid flip-flop buttons whose single label switches state (spell out the verb or use two buttons); and treat radio buttons as mutually exclusive groups of two or more with one always selected that suit a teaching role in infrequent dialogs, while a drop-down list is often better on a sovereign application's surface because it saves space.
Prevent catastrophic data loss from destructive actions by providing Undo (replace Reset with Undo) rather than a confirmation dialog.

Eliminate the Save Changes dialog and other file-mechanics interruptions, because managing disks and files is not a user goal: a dialog that is nearly always answered the same way is redundant and should be removed, and the proper time to reject changes is when they are made, through Undo, not at document close, which has no natural connection to discarding changes in the user's mental model.
Surface each error in context next to the responsible input with actionable fix instructions and 'double visual emphasis', and match the input's error style to the top-level error message.

For multiple errors, use one prominent top-level message that lists every error plus per-input double emphasis with resolution guidance in both places, since per-input emphasis alone can be missed below the fold on long forms.

Keep the number of message types minimal (one or two), avoid errors via no-error-state inputs, undo, and good defaults, show an error only when the user can't continue or the system failed, and never disguise marketing as an error.

When notification is genuinely warranted, do it well: for time-critical situations that truly require it (warning that after-hours trades cannot execute until the market reopens), notify the user obtrusively; and when an error dialog is truly unavoidable as a last resort, make it polite, illuminating, and helpful — never hinting the user caused the problem, making clear its scope, alternatives, default, and any information lost, and directly offering at least one button that implements a solution.

Use inline validation for answers people may get wrong (unique username, password strength), timing feedback only after the answer is complete, not validating answers users already know, and offering suggestions for broad valid sets—including quality indicators that steer better answers.
Apply inline-validation techniques well: generate suggestions from data the user already gave, reformat answers only after entry is finished, and show real-time counters for bounded inputs.

Serve minority needs with additional inputs that don't burden the majority: map inputs to prioritized use cases, expose extras via clearly worded user-activated triggers with easy removal, keep the approach consistent, and minimize page jumping.

Optimize sovereign applications, which monopolize the user's attention for long continuous full-screen periods, for perpetual intermediates: be generous with screen real estate and default to maximized, use a conservative minimal visual style, provide rich modeless feedback and rich input, map control placement to frequency of use, and maximize document views by default.

Handle selection-dependent inputs with these tested core rules: hide irrelevant controls until needed, keep initial options and their dependents in close proximity, maintain a clear association to the trigger, and avoid page jumping—these drive speed and satisfaction.

Choose the selection-dependent pattern by scale: page-level for large dependent sets, vertical tabs over horizontal, a drop-down list for more than 4–5 initial options, expose-within/below for only 1–3 dependents, and avoid exposed-inactive and exposed-groups.

Where possible eliminate the sign-up form via gradual engagement: let people use the service first and defer account creation, which teaches value and boosts adoption—give easy access to auto-created accounts, and don't just split a sign-up form across pages.
Consider single sign-on (OpenID, Live ID) to reduce duplicative sign-up and checkout forms, recognizing no clear standard has emerged.

Prioritize user goals over features and tasks: design product behavior to serve the reasons people use it, analyzing tasks only at the detail level after goals are understood, because a product built for business goals alone eventually fails.

Design to durable user goals rather than transient tasks, because goals change very slowly while tasks and activities depend on current technology, so task-only design yields at best incremental improvement and can trap the design in an outmoded technology model.
Aim to make users more effective, especially for productivity tools, by looking beyond their immediate tasks to identify the most important users and determine their goals and why.

Keep users' goals as the bedrock throughout the pressures of the development cycle, treating features and functions as a limited way to define a product, because a goal-directed process supplies a clear rationale that makes the design not guesswork or personal preference.

Avoid self-referential design that projects the designer's own goals, skills, and mental models onto a product, which is appropriate only for products aimed at people like the designer, and design for edge cases without ever making them the design focus, using personas to prioritize by asking whether the target persona will do it.

Serve user goals above nonuser goals: acknowledge and address customer, business, and technical goals but never let them form the design basis or be met at the user's expense, since technical goals are meaningless to a product's success unless derived from human-oriented goals.

Weigh the personal goals of the individuals who actually use the product above those of the corporation that employs them or the IT manager who supports them, because good design has meaning only for a person using a product for a purpose.

Beware designing primarily from workflow, which tends to yield a business implementation model that captures all the functionality but little of the humanity, and instead ground the design in user goals.

Define what the product will do before designing how it looks and behaves, treating requirements as human and business needs rather than features, because separating the problem from the solution gives the designer leverage to create a more compelling product and maximum flexibility against changing technology.

Take business goals and technical requirements into account during design, since a design must be built and deployed to have value, holding an active dialog among design, business, and engineering and not accepting claims that something is impossible at face value, because it often means impossible given the current schedule.

Design all aspects of a product before they are built, letting informed planning of the user experience precede construction even in a highly iterative process where building some parts can begin while others are still being designed.
Treat interaction design as the design of product behavior, not merely form, and use the resulting specification as a blueprint that tells engineers what to build and lets managers measure progress.

Perform design as a distinct discipline that precedes coding and testing, rather than applying it as a surface-level patch after construction, because complex interactive products require significant upfront design.

Design form and behavior in concert: when a product takes physical form, industrial designers must not develop form independently of behavior, and the interaction design team must stay available through development to make scaled-down trade-off decisions rather than leaving them to developers under time pressure.

Pretend the system is a considerate person to structure interaction-level details, apply general interaction principles and specific patterns rather than reinventing solutions, and obey established design standards unless you have a genuinely superior alternative.

Involve the programming team intimately throughout Refinement and construction, deliver a form and behavior specification detailed enough to code from, and stay vigilant that the design vision is translated faithfully into the final product.

Treat process, patterns, and principles as necessary but not sufficient for successful interaction design, which still requires the designer's spark of inventiveness and the judgment to tell whether a concept is good, and requires close collaboration with business decision makers, technologists, and other experience-affecting team members throughout the project rather than designing in a vacuum.

Separate the people who design a product from the people who build it, because a programmer faces a conflict of interest between ease of coding and ease of use and cannot advocate for user, business, and technology at once; design is a specialized skill, so do not ask users to design.

Structure the organization so design is an equal partner with engineering, marketing, and management, each holding well-defined responsibilities balanced by equal authority: design owns users' satisfaction, engineering builds to spec, marketing owns customer communication, and management owns profitability.

Distinguish users from customers, making the users who operate the product the main design focus while satisfying customers' purchasing goals for viability, and interview both groups as well as current and potential users.

Judge interface quality by context, since there is no objectively good user interface; applying one-size-fits-all principles is easier but not better, so understand the actual users, what they are doing, and their motivations before applying rules.

Use consistency and interface standards to raise learnability and throughput and cut errors and vendor costs, but treat standards as evolving guidelines rather than rigid rules: a product is only as good as its standard, and most standards govern syntax and look-and-feel rather than deeper behavior, so obey a standard unless an idiom is clearly significantly better to most target users in real working conditions, follow its spirit rather than its letter, and do not force uniformity across products whose users and goals differ.
Integrate the three design tools together, design principles, design patterns, and design processes, rather than relying on any one alone.

Recognize that design principles operate at several levels, values, conceptual, behavioral, and interface, and that for productivity tools the primary purpose of behavioral and interface principles is to minimize the user's cognitive, memory, visual, and physical work while increasing useful feedback.

Reason about a software product in terms of three distinct models, the implementation model of how it works in code, the user's mental model, and the represented model the designer chooses to present, remembering that the represented model is the aspect designers most control.

Base user interfaces on the user's mental model rather than the implementation model, making the represented model match the mental model as closely as possible and keeping it simpler than the actual implementation, because a represented model that follows the implementation too closely reduces the user's ability to learn and use the product.

Optimize for experts when the product is a specialized professional tool such as development tools, scientific instrumentation, or medical devices, and optimize for beginners when the product is used transiently or by people with disabilities such as public kiosks or assistive devices.

Serve experts and perpetual intermediates to their distinct needs: give experts fast shortcuts to their working set and new powerful features, and give intermediates their frequently used working set front and center with ToolTips and the reassurance that advanced features exist, remembering that experts disproportionately influence prospective buyers.

Achieve deep user understanding through ethnographic interviewing that combines one-on-one interviews with immersive observation in the user's own context, because people cannot accurately assess their own behavior away from that context; keep recording unobtrusive and verify any interpretation with the user.

Run ethnographic interviews without a fixed questionnaire, guiding users to examine their problems rather than propose solutions, steering away from product-implementation technology, encouraging specific stories, and avoiding leading questions.

Place usability testing late in the cycle to validate a concrete candidate design, using it for naming, organization, first-time use, and task effectiveness while recognizing it mainly assesses first-time use, and do the qualitative heavy lifting up front; ensure any test is measurable and its findings actionable.

Treat usability testing as a means to evaluate, not to create: conduct user research before ideation and testing after it, evaluate the design before coding begins or early enough to change it, and run formative tests late enough to have a concrete design yet early enough to adjust.

Employ the three persona-based scenario types, context, key path, and validation, and prefer scenarios over use cases for interaction design, because use cases catalog functional requirements but treat all interactions as equally likely and say nothing about presentation or priority, so use them only in late design validation.

Refine the design with key path scenarios describing the highest-frequency pathways and validation scenarios that poke holes by asking what-if in the order key-path-variant, necessary-use, then edge case; give infrequent necessary-use interactions pedagogy but not shortcuts, and handle edge cases without ever making them the design focus.

Build the Design Framework top-down, designing interaction, visual, and industrial frameworks in concert and starting from the big picture at low fidelity to stay focused on serving personas' goals, because focusing on pixels and widgets too early prevents a coherent framework and there is only one user experience, arising from form and behavior together.
Define the interaction framework in six iterative steps, beginning by choosing form factor, posture, and input methods driven by the usage context and the personas' attitudes and aptitudes.

Group functional and data elements to facilitate the persona's flow, placing compared or sequential items adjacent, and sketch the framework in a low-fidelity rectangles phase, keeping early renderings rough so it stays easy to discard one approach and try a superior one.

Explore visual design through three to five visual language studies, unlike the single optimal interaction framework, tying them to persona experience goals and brand keywords and adapting them to environment and aptitude, and never present a design approach you are not happy with, since stakeholders may choose it.

Represent the simplest complete solution by economy of form, using only the screens, widgets, and behaviors necessary and consistent with the personas' mental models, and pursue internal coherence so the design feels like a unified whole in balance rather than cobbled together from implementation-model pieces.

Treat visual interface design as a critical, unique communication discipline conducted alongside interaction and industrial design, not as afterthought skinning: place aesthetics within a functional framework driven by user-experience and business goals, and match the visual structure to the logical structure of the users' mental models and the program's behavior so the display communicates behavior clearly.
Keep tools close at hand, on palettes or toolbars for beginners and intermediates and via keyboard for experts, selectable in a single click or keystroke, and never make the user put tools away.

Do not force physically awkward idioms: because the menu is beginners' primary control yet is hard to operate (requiring click-and-drag), support single-click menu operation and provide an alternative non-drag idiom such as a toolbar button for any function used more than rarely; keep the working set of modal palette tools small, since selecting and deselecting them does not scale for intermediates; and give a charged cursor a clear visual indication of its modal state and a good cancel idiom, allowing either a single click for a default-sized object or a drag-rectangle for a custom size.

Design toolbars to give experienced users fast, visible, immediate access to frequently used functions rather than duplicating the descriptive menu: use images on toolbars and text on menus deliberately, since text is precise but slow (suiting teaching) while a pictograph is ambiguous until learned but then recognized fast (suiting quick access); a butcon's icon need only be recognizable once learned, with its purpose taught through ToolTips (well-timed with about a one-second lag) rather than by labeling it with both text and image, which costs too many pixels; and disable inapplicable toolbar controls by graying them out rather than making them disappear, because users remember toolbar layouts by position.
Provide modeless feedback by building status and effect information into the structure of the interface rather than interrupting the user with a modal dialog.

Prefer modal dialogs where a dialog is used, because they are easiest for users to understand — clearly saying to stop and deal with this now, since freezing application state is what makes them simpler — while modeless dialogs are harder to design and use because the selection can change during their lifetime and their scope is unclear; almost never use a system-modal dialog that halts the entire system (reserve it for catastrophic occurrences); and when a modeless dialog is used, visually differentiate it from modal dialogs and give it a single, consistently placed Close button that is never disabled and never relabeled, relying on the application-wide Undo rather than a Cancel.

Keep users constantly informed with rich visual modeless feedback — information about the status and attributes of processes and objects that is rich, visual, and always displayed without a mode shift, the way a car dashboard is — to help users avoid mistakes and all but eliminate dialogs; recognize that such feedback is not for beginners because it takes work to discover and decode, so keep menus and dialogs as support and make any feedback used to warn of serious trouble extraordinarily clear; and prefer positive audible feedback (a success sound whose absence signals a problem) over negative beeps that act as insulting public alarms.

Avoid unnecessary reporting and never stop the proceedings to report normalcy, instead doing the work, issuing reassuring clues, and taking a good-enough first step the user can adjust rather than requiring the user to direct every action in advance.

Do not stop the proceedings with idiocy: eliminate high-excise error and confirmation dialogs, allow input wherever you have output so a user can change a displayed value in place, and root out common excise traps such as forcing window switches, remembering file locations, reentering settings, asking permission, or confirming actions.

Do, don't ask: give software the courage of its convictions backed by user research rather than interrupting with alerts and confirmation dialogs, because confirmations reflect the implementation model, pass the buck to users, and only work when unexpected (routine ones get dismissed by rote like the boy who cried wolf, so a real danger warning is ignored) — instead make all actions reversible, even deleting or overwriting a file by moving it to a holding area first, and let the user issue Undo on the rare occasion an action was wrong, keeping them informed through modeless feedback rather than stopping the proceedings.

Treat navigation as largely excise and minimize it, recognizing that navigation among multiple windows, views, or pages is the most disorienting kind, which sovereign applications avoid by placing all main interactions in a single primary view with panes.

Use adjacent panes to reduce navigation, placing panes that support drag-and-drop next to each other, avoid splitting one facility across tabbed panes since that increases excise, reserve tabs for a multi-document work area or mutually exclusive supporting panes, group frequently used tools spatially while reserving menus for infrequent commands, and minimize scrolling.

Improve navigation by reducing the number of places a user must go, keeping windows, views, panes, and controls to the minimum needed, providing signposts as persistent objects, overviews, appropriate control-to-function mapping, interface inflection, and by avoiding hierarchies.

Avoid multi-window navigation schemes for moving between programs: the overlapping-sheets window metaphor does not scale beyond about three applications and causes lost-window confusion, and multiple windows sharing a small screen (overlapping or tiled) is not a good general solution, so prefer full-screen applications with a minimal switching mechanism such as a taskbar; inside a sovereign application, however, multipaned windows that display related information in adjacent panes reduce navigation and window-management excise to almost nil and are practically a requirement.

Make the normal state of a sovereign application a maximized full-screen window, with little reason to pluralize it except to support switching or dragging data between programs, and use a multiple-document interface only when users genuinely need multiple related views together in one environment, not when it forces them to manage little windows inside a big one or destroys orientation permanency through changing menus — often clean full-window switching is better.

Give metaphors, especially physical and spatial ones, an extremely limited place in software design, and choose among the three interface paradigms by preferring the idiomatic, based on learning how to accomplish things, over the difficult implementation-centric and risky metaphoric paradigms; avoid implementation-centric and org-chart-centric interfaces that force users to understand internal structure, because most people would rather be successful than knowledgeable.

Give metaphors an extremely limited place in interface design: they do not scale as a process grows in complexity, depend on cultural associations the user may not share, and offer only a small first-use learnability boost while permanently limiting software power for the intermediates users soon become.

Never bend the interface to fit a metaphor; use a metaphor only when a truly appropriate and powerful one falls in your lap, because good metaphors are hard to find for software's processes and relationships, global metaphors add navigation overhead, and extending a metaphor tempts you toward an obsolete mechanical model — the Macintosh succeeded through overall design detail, not its desktop metaphor.

Honor manual affordances: use simulated-3D shading to signal that an element can be manipulated, but because a virtual affordance shows only that a control is manipulable and not what it does, always label controls with text or icons, and deliver on the contract an affordance makes by responding visually when actuated and doing the reasonable work the control's legend describes — never bait-and-switch.

Let the shape, behavior, and affordance of controls drive the visual style so aesthetic considerations never interfere with meaning or the ability to interact, controlling stylized elements especially carefully in sovereign applications.

Make direct manipulation succeed through rich visual feedback: provide a visual representation of the objects of concern, visible gestural mechanisms for acting on them instead of text commands, and immediately visible results; render data, objects, controls, and cursors with enough graphic detail to be manipulable, since users can directly manipulate only what is displayed; and decide from the personas' skills and contexts what should be manipulated directly versus handled more indirectly, because direct-manipulation idioms are easily taught and seldom forgotten yet can demand motor coordination.

Design storage and retrieval from the users' mental models and usage contexts rather than exposing the file system: because storage and retrieval need not be linked digitally as they are physically, do not hand users the storage system as the retrieval system, and since positional (where it was left) and identity (its name) retrieval both burden memory, provide associative, attribute-based retrieval so users can find documents by their contents and meaningful properties expressed the way they think.

Reduce the burden of organizing files: automatically remember many document attributes (creating application, format, size, edit/print/email history, usage frequency), return search results fast by indexing content during idle time, and also let users tag or manually assign attributes to form a folksonomy that fills gaps and defines dynamically overlapping sets, which is especially valuable in collaborative contexts.

Separate the storage system from the retrieval system rather than forcing users to conform to a rigid relational schema: keep records in a database-like digital soup that accepts any record and returns a token, build retrieval as an unlimited number of attribute indices each keyed to one concept, fill those indices both by automatic extraction and by easy manual pointers, and never demand that users configure their information in advance, because they rarely can express their needs ahead of time and often change their minds.

Present storage according to the user's single-document mental model rather than the file system's implementation model of two copies (one in memory, one on disk) that both belong to the application: hide the file system's existence, use a unified file model that treats the document as one thing and leaves disk/memory writing to the file system, and avoid the Save As trap that conflates naming and placing a file, cannot rename or relocate the current document, and can silently discard recent changes.

Model Undo the least like its implementation and the most like the user's mental model, because Undo exists exclusively for humans, who make mistakes: treat everything the user does as valid and reasonable rather than as error, recognize that Undo's primary purpose is to support exploration (reassuring users and encouraging experimentation), and understand that it serves the necessary condition of trustworthiness rather than directly advancing a goal.

Design Undo to satisfy the several mental models users bring — a panic button, a deleted-data store, a stack of reversible operations — make it a global, program-wide function that undoes the last action however it was performed, keep it available after a document is saved, save the undo buffer with the document, and never hint through visual, audible, or textual cues that Undo signals a user failure.

Exploit richer reversal idioms: treat a paired Undo-Redo as a comparison or what-if tool and consider a single Compare control that follows the user's apply-versus-don't-apply mental model, and offer category-specific incremental Undo (like Backspace undoing only typed characters while ignoring intervening functions), which works because everything is visible and consistent with the user's mental model.

Audit the application for operations that only masquerade as undo-proof (renaming a file) versus those genuinely irreversible (a sent email), making the former undoable; and where business rules or institutional policy forbid undoing an action, still serve human goals by providing a way to reverse or adjust it while leaving an audit trail.

Support precise object positioning and manipulation: dedicate a specific area such as a title bar to repositioning so the object's drag idiom stays free for other functions (with explicit pliancy hinting), offer a meta-key constrained drag that locks movement to a single axis, assist alignment with guides and dynamic smart guides and snapping, and use resize handles that double as selection indicators (vertex handles for polylines, Bezier handles for curves) — remembering that handles obscure the object they mark, making them poor permanent controls best replaced by frame or corner resizers for windows.

Provide the right specialized manipulation idioms: offer both a bounding-box idiom for proportional scaling and a vertex-editing idiom for fine-tuning a freeform object's shape, since each serves a distinct purpose, and implement object connection (dragging a line or arrow between objects) with rubber-banding feedback, active hinting that highlights valid targets as the connection is dragged over them, and a convenient way to cancel.

For manipulating 3D objects on a 2D screen, treat rich modeless feedback (baseline grids, depth cueing, shadows, poles, color-coded guidelines) as a necessity for conveying position and movement, use multiple viewpoints to aid alignment despite the mental triangulation they require, and address the picking problem of selecting occluded objects with techniques such as a hover menu of candidates, per-facet pliancy hinting, and fluid navigation (mapping zoom and orbit to the scroll wheel) supported by a thumbnail absolute view to keep users oriented.

Treat each window, pane, or dialog box as a separate room and do not add one unless it serves a purpose existing windows cannot: put functions in the window where they are used, so a task integral to the application's purpose belongs in the main window rather than a dialog (one of the most frequently violated UI principles), reserve a separate room such as a dialog for functions performed outside the user's normal sequence (purging a database, importing clip art), and avoid windows pollution from putting a single function in each dialog, since a goal involves a series of functions whose connections many windows cannot show.

Put primary interactions in the primary window and let dialog boxes play only a secondary role, because forcing users to bounce between the main window and its dialogs leads to fatigue: reserve dialogs for functions out of the main flow — anything confusing, dangerous, dislocating, or rarely used — giving a big friendly Cancel button and room for protective and explanatory information, and use dialogs to gather the controls and information about a single domain object or a single function in one place, reducing the navigation excise of hunting through the interface.

Prefer toolbars, palettes, and sidebars over modeless dialogs, because they are modeless without the conundrums — visually distinct, omnipresent so they need no terminating control, efficient in screen space, and not covering what they operate on; and since repositioning windows is never a user's goal, replace free-floating modeless dialogs (which create window-management excise) with docked palettes, sidebars, task panes, or a properties area that provide the same modeless interactivity while retaining the user's context.

Treat menus as a pedagogic vector whose primary role is to teach new users, remind those who have forgotten, and provide access to infrequently used functions — not as the main way normal users perform everyday functions, which toolbars and direct manipulation serve better — so flatten deep sequential menu hierarchies into monocline grouping (aided by dialogs that gather subchoices) to improve scanability, make menu text verbose and jargon-free (Open Report rather than Open) and the menus complete so a scan reveals the program's full scope, and support users moving ad hoc and piecemeal from beginner to expert by reading the menu for unfamiliar functions while invoking familiar ones with memorized shortcuts.

Do not blindly accept the standard File, Edit, and Help menu structure, which reflects implementation-model thinking and names that sound like tools rather than goals; organize menus by users' mental models and a goal-directed structure, naming the primary menu after the document type when appropriate.

Design menu structure and item behavior for clarity: use cascading hierarchical menus only in sophisticated sovereign applications for rarely used functions or as a secondary vector (with a wide movement threshold), avoid adaptive menus that hide infrequent items (which studies show slow users down and which they overwhelmingly dislike), avoid bang/immediate menus whose title executes a function (immediate commands belong on toolbars), gray out inapplicable menu items to improve the menu's teaching value, and use a checkmark item that is clearly checked or unchecked rather than a flip-flop item that shows the state not currently chosen.

Provide multiple parallel command vectors — menus, toolbars, keyboard accelerators, and direct manipulation — so users of different skill sets can command the program the way that suits them, giving immediate vectors to the minimal working set of frequently used functions identified from persona scenarios and pedagogic vectors to beginners, and understanding that information in the world (menus, dialogs) is dependable but slow while information in the head (accelerators) is fast but must be learned, so beginners rely on world vectors and experts increasingly on head vectors; as an exception, deny dangerous commands like Erase All easy parallel vectors and protect them within menus and dialogs like hidden ejector-seat levers.

Build strong keyboard and cross-vector support: show the same identifying icon on a menu item as on its corresponding toolbar butcon so users build a visual language connecting the two, create good keyboard accelerators by following platform standards and assigning them to functions in everyone's daily use (shown to the right of each menu item, triaged by always/never/maybe daily use), and treat access keys or mnemonics as not optional, providing a complete, consistent keyboard equivalent of every menu command.

Build a memorization vector into the interface — a path by which users learn the fast head vector corresponding to each slow world vector — through accelerators shown beside menu items, underlined mnemonics, and a Shortcuts item on the Help menu rather than buried documentation, and show each function's identifying icon on every artifact that deals with it (every menu, butcon, dialog, help text, and printed page), because a memorization vector of consistent visual symbols is the most effective yet underexploited technique.

Recognize the four goal-directed dialog types — property dialogs to view and change a selected object's attributes, function dialogs to initiate and configure a single function, process dialogs to report a busy internal function, and bulletin dialogs for unrequested messages — separate configuring a function from invoking it while linking them seamlessly (so a routine task need not confront the full complexity of options), and whenever an application begins a perceptibly time-consuming process, inform the user that it is busy but otherwise normal, or the silence will read as rudeness or a crash.

Avoid dialog anti-patterns: never use transitory dialogs that take themselves down for errors or confirmations, because the message must stop the program so the user definitely gets it; minimize bulletin dialogs (errors, alerts, confirmations), which serve the application at the user's expense, unlike requested property and function dialogs; group a tabbed dialog with a meaningful breadth-or-depth rationale and split stacked tabs into several dialogs with fewer tabs each; and treat cascading dialogs (one summoning another with its own OK/Cancel) as confusing symptoms of excessive complexity and structural flaws in the interaction framework.

Understand that error message boxes stop the proceedings with idiocy and mostly report the program's own inability to work flexibly rather than a genuinely serious problem: most bulletins fire when the computer is confused by out-of-bounds or out-of-sequence input rather than a substantive user mistake, so the software should assume the human input is correct and work harder to reconcile it — accepting the transaction with modeless feedback that something is not yet recognized and letting the user supply missing information before the session ends, the way manual systems work — recognizing that error messages do not prevent user errors, they only prevent the program from getting into trouble.

Eliminate error messages by redesigning the software to be immune to the problem and to prevent error conditions from arising — treating an error message as an abnormal idiom of last resort — using bounded controls such as drop-downs and lists so users cannot enter bad values, and making the application smart enough to avoid unnecessary demands by supplying known values itself, remembering prior files, and reading the date from the internal clock.

Reduce reliance on documentation through design: offer a gallery of ready-to-use templates so users can pick a premade starting design and make small changes, because a blank slate intimidates most people; and treat online help as a reference tool for perpetual intermediates already using the product who want to expand their horizons, not as a crutch or a resource aimed at beginners, letting good design greatly reduce users' need for help.

Design help as a reference for perpetual intermediates: make the index the priority of any reference document, generating it from an examination of the program and all its features rather than only the help text, with as many synonyms as possible and the goal-directed terms a user would actually search for; include a Shortcuts digest of tools and keyboard commands and an overview describing each feature's scope, effect, power, and trade-offs; and rely on ToolTips as modeless online help, which is incredibly effective, unlike a standard separate help program that covers up the application and cannot point at on-screen objects the way a helpful person would.
